title: Find your sites on the map
description: Learn what map pins represent, how to correct a position, and why map visibility is not edit permission.

chapters.title: Give a site a real position

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our fictional team looks after a shop and a warehouse. A list of names is useful, but a map would make the locations clearer. What puts a site on Hub's map?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The map uses coordinates saved with the site's address. Choose an address suggestion when creating or editing a site, and Hub stores the address and its position. Sites without valid coordinates won't appear just because they have a name.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can the browser help locate us?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It can, with permission and the appropriate secure browser context. Address suggestions also depend on the deployment's Maps and Places configuration. If suggestions are missing, check that setup rather than repeatedly changing the site's name.

chapters.title: Read the overview without moving sites

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The warehouse is close to another site, and I see a group of pins. Have they been merged?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Nearby sites are visually grouped as you zoom out so the map stays readable. Zoom in or inspect the group to separate the locations. The map is an overview of accessible sites, not a tool that combines their resources.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And dragging around the overview won't accidentally relocate the warehouse?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. The overview is read-only. Browsing the map and changing a site's saved coordinates are separate actions. Pins show a site's initials and colour to help identify it as you explore.

chapters.title: Correct the entrance, keep the address

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our warehouse pin is close, but it points to the wrong entrance. Do we need a made-up address to fix that?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Use the site's location editor to fine-tune its coordinates, then save. That changes the position while keeping the formatted address and its other metadata. Before saving, Reset can restore the position from the most recently selected address.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the address answers where the site is, while the corrected pin can make that answer more precise?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. The guide supports both moving the map under a fixed centre pin and entering valid coordinates. Choose the approach that lets your team check the location accurately.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: If a colleague sees the pin, can they change it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not simply because it's visible. The map shows sites available in the current account and project context. Editing uses the site's existing access rules. Keep operational access separate from the convenience of a geographic view.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Pick one site, confirm its address and coordinates, and inspect its pin. If it's absent, check the saved position and access. If the background tiles or suggestions fail, the guide has deployment-specific checks without asking you to expose secret credentials in the browser.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
